knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Feasibility Does Not Ensure Barrier Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict feasibility alone does not guarantee existence of logarithmic-barrier minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{-x:x\ge0\}\), the strict domain is \(D=(0,\infty)\) and \(\phi_\mu(x)=-x-\mu\log x\). For every \(\mu>0\), \(\phi_\mu(x)\to-\infty\) as \(x\to\infty\), so the barrier minimizer set is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly feasible unbounded improving direction can make every barrier subproblem unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: The inequality is \(x\ge0\), with strict domain \(D=(0,\infty)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barrier Hessian and Sharp Strict-Convexity Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-space curvature criterion for the logarithmic-barrier QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(x\in D\), let \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(h-Gx)\). Then \(\nabla^2\phi_\mu(x)=Q+\mu G^{\mathsf T}S^{-2}G\), and for \(d\in\ker A\), \[d^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2\phi_\mu(x)d=d^{\mathsf T}Qd+\mu\|S^{-1}Gd\|_2^2.\] Hence the Hessian is positive definite on \(\ker A\), and the barrier objective is strictly convex on the equality-feasible affine space, exactly when \(\ker A\cap\ker Q\cap\ker G=\{0\}\). Under this condition any existing minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic curvature and constraint-normal curvature combine to give a sharp nullspace test for strict convexity and uniqueness.

notation.meaning: diagonal matrix of positive inequality slacks

knowledge_statements.title: Barrier Hessian and Sharp Strict-Convexity Test
Logarithmic-Barrier QP Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained logarithmic barriers for strictly feasible QPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\), define \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) and the strict domain \(D=\{x:Ax=b,\ Gx<h\}\). For every \(\mu>0\), the logarithmic-barrier QP is
\[\min_{x\in D}\ \phi_\mu(x):=f(x)-\mu\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\bigl(h_i-G_i x\bigr).\]
The collection \(\{\phi_\mu:\mu>0\}\), together with its minimizer sets \(X(\mu)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}\phi_\mu(x)\), is the logarithmic-barrier QP family. If \(Q\) is positive definite on \(\ker A\), every nonempty \(X(\mu)\) is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The family adds a weighted negative-log penalty for every positive inequality slack while retaining equality constraints exactly.
assumptions_latex: Each row \(G_i\) corresponds to one inequality.
review_flags: No supplied source locator directly covers logarithmic-barrier QPs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The barrier family is coherently defined, the strict domain and parameter are explicit, and the conditional uniqueness statement follows the appropriate equality-feasible curvature condition. The definition has no supporting source reference or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity and Derivative of the Primal Central Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local smoothness and sensitivity equation for a regular primal central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s(\mu)=h-Gx(\mu)>0\), \(S(\mu)=\operatorname{Diag}(s(\mu))\), and \(H_\mu=Q+\mu G^{\mathsf T}S(\mu)^{-2}G\). If \[K_\mu=\begin{bmatrix}H_\mu&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\] is nonsingular, then \((x(\mu),y(\mu))\) is locally differentiable and \[K_\mu\begin{bmatrix}x'(\mu)\\y'(\mu)\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}G^{\mathsf T}s(\mu)^{-1}\\0\end{bmatrix}.\] If the bordered matrix is singular, this stationarity system alone does not guarantee such a regular local parameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a regular path point, the primal path is differentiable and its parameter derivative is obtained from one bordered-Hessian solve.
assumptions_latex: Each barrier problem on an open parameter interval has a path point x(\mu) and equality multiplier y(\mu).
The displayed bordered matrix is nonsingular at the parameter considered.

notation.meaning: barrier Hessian at the path point

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity and Derivative of the Primal Central Path
Primal Central Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal trajectory of unique logarithmic-barrier minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the logarithmic-barrier QP family, assume that for every \(\mu>0\) the barrier objective has a unique minimizer. The primal central path is the mapping \(x:(0,\infty)\to D\) defined by
\[x(\mu)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}\left\{\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x-\mu\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log(h_i-G_i x)\right\}.\]
Equivalently, \(x(\mu)\) is accompanied by an equality multiplier \(y(\mu)\) and satisfies \(Ax(\mu)=b\) and
\[Qx(\mu)+c+A^{\mathsf T}y(\mu)+\mu G^{\mathsf T}(h-Gx(\mu))^{-1}=0,\]
where the inverse is componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal central path traces the unique minimizers of the logarithmic-barrier QPs as the barrier parameter varies.
assumptions_latex: The strict feasible domain is nonempty.
Each barrier subproblem has a unique minimizer.
The equality constraints admit Lagrange multipliers at those minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu\mapsto x(\mu)\) is the primal central path.

notation.meaning: equality multiplier at the path point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimizer trajectory and its stationarity characterization are consistent with the stated logarithmic barrier, and definition is the correct content kind. No cited source or locator supports the characterization and its regularity assumptions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient Conditions for a Unique Primal-Dual Central Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness at each positive barrier parameter under strict convexity, equality independence, and strict primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(Q\succ0\), \(A\) has full row rank, and \(\{x:Ax=b,\ Gx<h\}\neq\varnothing\). For every \(\mu>0\), the logarithmic-barrier QP has a unique minimizer \(x(\mu)\). With \(s=h-Gx(\mu)\) and \(z_i=\mu/s_i\), there is a unique \(y(\mu)\) such that \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu),z(\mu))\) satisfies the primal-dual central-path equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity, independent equality constraints, and strict primal feasibility ensure a unique primal-dual central point for every positive barrier parameter.
review_flags: These are sufficient, not necessary, conditions for uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Sufficient Conditions for a Unique Primal-Dual Central Point
Primal-Dual Central Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbed KKT trajectory for a convex inequality-constrained QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\) and \(\mu>0\), a primal-dual central-path point is a quadruple \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu),z(\mu))\) satisfying
\[Ax=b,\qquad Gx+s=h,\qquad Qx+c+A^{\mathsf T}y+G^{\mathsf T}z=0,\]
\[s>0,\qquad z>0,\qquad S z=\mu\mathbf 1,\]
where \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\). The primal-dual central path is the set, or the parameterized trajectory when the solution is unique, of all such quadruples as \(\mu\) ranges over \((0,\infty)\). Its duality gap is \(s^{\mathsf T}z=m\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-dual central path consists of feasible positive primal-dual points satisfying complementarity products equal to the barrier parameter.
assumptions_latex: Strictly feasible primal and dual points exist.
The displayed perturbed KKT system has a solution for each considered \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S z=\mu\mathbf1\) and \(s^{\mathsf T}z=m\mu\) along the primal-dual central path.
review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports the perturbed-KKT definition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The perturbed KKT system, positivity conditions, and duality-gap identity consistently define the primal-dual central path. The selected definition kind fits the leaf, but the record contains no authoritative citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-dual central path for a linearly constrained convex quadratic program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-QP specialization of the perturbed slack-form KKT system; the internally inconsistent displayed Newton equation is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min_x\ \frac12x^TGx+g^Tx\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax\ge b,\qquad G=G^T\succeq0,\] and introduce \(y=Ax-b\). With \(Y=\operatorname{diag}(y)\), \(\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)\), and \[F(x,y,\lambda)=\begin{bmatrix}Gx-A^T\lambda+g\\Ax-y-b\\Y\Lambda e\end{bmatrix},\] the primal-dual central path is \[\mathcal C=\left\{(x_\tau,y_\tau,\lambda_\tau):F(x_\tau,y_\tau,\lambda_\tau)=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\\tau e\end{bmatrix},\ (y_\tau,\lambda_\tau)>0,\ \tau>0\right\}.\] Thus the path retains stationarity and slack feasibility while replacing complementarity \(Y\Lambda e=0\) by the positive perturbation \(Y\Lambda e=\tau e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex quadratic program with linear inequalities, introduce nonnegative slacks. The primal-dual central path consists of strictly positive slack-multiplier triples satisfying stationarity and slack feasibility, with every complementary product equal to the same positive parameter.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\quad g\in\mathbb R^n,\quad b\in\mathbb R^m

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of a bounded primal central path to a unique QP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a convex QP with a nonempty strict feasible domain and a finite attained optimum. For every \(\mu>0\), let \(x(\mu)\) be a primal logarithmic-barrier minimizer. Assume that \(\{x(\mu):0<\mu\le\bar\mu\}\) is bounded for some \(\bar\mu>0\). If the original QP has the unique primal optimal solution \(x_*\), then
\[\lim_{\mu\downarrow0}x(\mu)=x_*.\]
This conclusion concerns only the primal path and does not assert uniqueness of limiting multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the small-parameter logarithmic-barrier path is bounded and the convex QP has a unique primal optimizer, the path converges to that optimizer as the barrier parameter tends to zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representation Dependence of the Selected Face Center
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation dependence of logarithmic-barrier selection on a nonunique optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every point of \(F=[0,1]\) be optimal. For the strict representation \(x>0\), \(1-x>0\), the barrier minimizer is \(x(\mu)=1/2\). Duplicating \(x>0\) gives the equivalent representation with barrier term \(-\mu[2\log x+\log(1-x)]\), whose minimizer is \(\widetilde x(\mu)=2/3\). Thus the selected point depends on inequality multiplicities even though the closed feasible set and optimal set are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicating a redundant inequality moves the barrier-selected center from one half to two thirds without changing the feasible or optimal set.
assumptions_latex: The closed feasible set is represented either by \(x\ge0,\ 1-x\ge0\) or by duplicating \(x\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Dependence of the Selected Face Center

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Convex-QP Optimal Set Need Not Be a Polyhedral Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for nonunique central-path limit statements that assume the entire optimal set is a face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=[-1,1]\times[0,1]\) and minimize \(f(x)=x_1^2\). The optimal set is \(S=\{0\}\times[0,1]\), which is not a face of \(P\): for every \(t\in(0,1)\), \((0,t)=\tfrac12(-1,t)+\tfrac12(1,t)\), while neither endpoint belongs to \(S\). For the logarithmic barrier containing one term for each of the four displayed box inequalities, the barrier-path point is \(x(\mu)=(0,1/2)\) for every \(\mu>0\). Thus a central path can select a distinguished point of a nonfacial optimal set, and a general limit theorem cannot assume without an additional hypothesis that every convex-QP optimal set is a face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex QP can have a nonfacial line-segment optimal set while its logarithmic barrier selects the segment's midpoint.
assumptions_latex: The barrier contains one logarithm for each of the four displayed box inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S=\{0\}\times[0,1]\text{ is not a face of }P,\qquad x(\mu)=(0,\tfrac12).
knowledge_statements.title: A Convex-QP Optimal Set Need Not Be a Polyhedral Face

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constant-Objective Barrier Path Is the Representation Analytic Center
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactly solvable nonunique-limit regime for a fixed logarithmic-barrier representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\overline P=\{x:Ax=b,\ Gx\le h\}\) and \(P^\circ=\{x:Ax=b,\ Gx<h\}\), with \(P^\circ\ne\varnothing\). Fix this inequality representation and define \(\phi(x)=-\sum_i\log(h_i-G_i x)\) on \(P^\circ\). Suppose \(\phi\) has a unique minimizer \(x^{\mathrm{ac}}\) on \(P^\circ\), and the QP objective \(f\) is constant on \(\overline P\). Then, for every \(\mu>0\), the barrier subproblem \(\min_{x\in P^\circ}f(x)+\mu\phi(x)\) has the unique solution \(x(\mu)=x^{\mathrm{ac}}\). Consequently \(x(\mu)\to x^{\mathrm{ac}}\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every feasible point is optimal, a fixed logarithmic-barrier representation selects its analytic center for every positive barrier parameter.
assumptions_latex: The fixed-representation logarithmic barrier has a unique minimizer.

notation.meaning: Closed feasible set and its strict relative interior for the displayed representation.
Logarithmic barrier for the fixed inequality representation.

If \(x(\mu)\) minimizes \(f+\mu\phi\) on \(P^\circ\) for every \(\mu>0\), then every accumulation point of \(x(\mu)\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\) minimizes \(f\) on \(\overline P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every cluster point of the logarithmic-barrier path is optimal on a compact feasible set, although the selected optimizer need not yet be identified.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Barrier Selection on an Unbounded Optimal Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence boundary for a primal logarithmic-barrier path when the nonunique optimal set is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the constant objective \(f(x)=0\) on \(P^\circ=(0,\infty)\), represented by \(x>0\), with logarithmic barrier \(\phi(x)=-\log x\). For every \(\mu>0\), \[\inf_{x>0}\{f(x)+\mu\phi(x)\}=-\infty.\] Hence no barrier minimizer \(x(\mu)\) exists, although every feasible point is optimal for the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbounded nonunique optimal set may make the logarithmic-barrier subproblem unbounded, so a selected path limit need not exist.

notation.meaning: Logarithmic barrier for the displayed inequality representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Barrier Selection on an Unbounded Optimal Set
Nonunique Optimal-Face Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Analytic-center selection on a bounded non-singleton optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the feasible set \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ Gx\le h\}\) be a bounded polytope with nonempty interior relative to \(Ax=b\), and let a convex QP attain its minimum on the non-singleton face \(F\). Define \(I_F=\{i:G_i x=h_i\text{ for every }x\in F\}\). If the relative analytic center
\[x_F^{\mathrm{ac}}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\operatorname{relint}F}-\sum_{i\notin I_F}\log(h_i-G_i x)\]
is unique, then the primal logarithmic-barrier path satisfies \(x(\mu)\to x_F^{\mathrm{ac}}\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\). Thus the barrier selects a distinguished relative-interior point rather than an arbitrary optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded problem with multiple optima, the logarithmic barrier approaches the relative analytic center of the optimal face.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a bounded polytope with a relative Slater point.
The convex QP optimal set is the non-singleton face \(F\).
The displayed relative analytic center is unique.

notation.meaning: inequalities identically active on the optimal face
relative analytic center of the optimal face

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representation-Relative Perturbation Selector on a Nonunique Optimal Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract vanishing-regularization theorem proposed as a substitute for a logarithmic-barrier limit theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be compact, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and let \(\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous and bounded below. Set \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}_{X}f\), assume \(S\cap\operatorname{dom}\phi\ne\varnothing\), and choose \(x_\mu\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{X}(f+\mu\phi)\) for every \(\mu>0\). Then every accumulation point of \(x_\mu\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\) belongs to \(S_\phi=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}\phi(x)\). If \(S_\phi=\{x^\phi\}\), then \(x_\mu\to x^\phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vanishing lower-semicontinuous regularizer selects its minimizers over the original optimal set when the stated minimizers exist.
assumptions_latex: \phi\text{ is lower semicontinuous and bounded below}

notation.meaning: Minimizers of the regularizer over the original optimal set.

children.top_down_role: Trajectory behavior near weakly complementary or degenerate optimal faces.

notation.meaning: slack for the constraint that x is nonnegative
nonnegative multiplier for the constraint that x is nonnegative

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional convex QP realizing fractional slack and multiplier rates at a degenerate optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\ge0}\tfrac12x^2\). With slack \(s=x\) and multiplier \(z\ge0\), the perturbed KKT equations are \(x-z=0\) and \(xz=\mu\). Their positive solution is \(x(\mu)=s(\mu)=z(\mu)=\sqrt\mu\). The unique optimum is \(x^*=0\), where \(s^*=z^*=0\), so neither member of the complementary pair is \(O(\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar convex QP has a degenerate central path on which both slack and multiplier decay as the square root of the barrier parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Square-Root Central-Path Rate in a Degenerate Convex QP
knowledge_statements.title: Square-Root Central-Path Rate in a Degenerate Convex QP

notation.meaning: Jacobian of stationarity and perturbed complementarity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conditioning deterioration for the scalar square-root-rate example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x,z)=(x-z,xz-\mu)=0\), the Jacobian at \(x=z=\sqrt\mu\) is \(J(\mu)=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\ \sqrt\mu&\sqrt\mu\end{bmatrix}\). Its singular values are \(\sqrt2\) and \(\sqrt{2\mu}\), hence \(\kappa_2(J(\mu))=\mu^{-1/2}\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the scalar degenerate example, the central-path Jacobian becomes ill conditioned exactly at the inverse square-root rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Central-Path Jacobian Conditioning
Degeneracy-Induced Path Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of linear identification rates without strict complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Along a primal-dual central path, each inequality satisfies \(s_i(\mu)z_i(\mu)=\mu\). If a limiting KKT point is degenerate at index \(i\), meaning \(s_i^*=z_i^*=0\), complementarity alone permits balanced or fractional rates
\[s_i(\mu)=\mu^\alpha,\qquad z_i(\mu)=\mu^{1-\alpha},\qquad 0<\alpha<1.\]
Hence neither \(s_i(\mu)=O(\mu)\) nor \(z_i(\mu)=O(\mu)\) follows. The usual strict-complementarity separation between vanishing slacks and positive multipliers is lost, so activity prediction based on a uniform linear threshold can remain ambiguous and the path Jacobian may become increasingly ill-conditioned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When both limiting slack and multiplier vanish, complementarity permits fractional rates and destroys uniform active-set separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy prevents complementarity alone from implying \(s_i(\mu)=O(\mu)\) or \(z_i(\mu)=O(\mu)\).
review_flags: A source is needed for the algorithmic and conditioning implications of degenerate path rates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic observation that complementarity alone permits fractional rates is correct and fits a degeneracy failure boundary. A source is required for extending that observation to activity-prediction ambiguity and possible central-path Jacobian ill-conditioning.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Accuracy and Limit Optimality of Exact Barrier Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier-specific accuracy and asymptotic correctness without an iteration-rate claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\), assume strict primal feasibility, and let \(x(\mu)\) exactly minimize each logarithmic-barrier subproblem. If the original optimum \(f^*\) is attained, then \(0\le f(x(\mu))-f^*\le m\mu\). Consequently, every feasible accumulation point of \(x(\mu_k)\) for \(\mu_k\downarrow0\) is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact barrier minimizers have objective error at most m mu, and their accumulation points are optimal.
assumptions_latex: Each barrier subproblem is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy and Limit Optimality of Exact Barrier Minimizers
Primal Barrier Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer barrier-parameter iteration with primal subproblem solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input \(Q,c,A,b,G,h\), a strictly feasible \(x^0\), parameters \(\mu_0>0\), \(0<\theta<1\), and tolerances \(\eta_k\downarrow0\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), approximately solve
\[\min_{Ax=b,\,Gx<h}\ \tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x-\mu_k\sum_i\log(h_i-G_i x)\]
from \(x^k\), producing a strictly feasible \(x^{k+1}\) whose equality-constrained first-order residual is at most \(\eta_k\). Stop and output \(x^{k+1}\) when the chosen primal optimality and barrier-gap tests are at most \(\varepsilon\); otherwise set \(\mu_{k+1}=\theta\mu_k\) and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal barrier method repeatedly solves strictly feasible log-barrier QPs while decreasing the barrier parameter.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a strictly positive iterate, solve the primal-dual Newton system first with complementarity right-hand side \(-XZe\), obtaining \((\Delta x^{\rm aff},\Delta y^{\rm aff},\Delta z^{\rm aff})\). Let \(\alpha_{\rm aff}\) be the largest common step preserving nonnegativity, set \(\mu=x^Tz/n\), \(\mu_{\rm aff}=(x+\alpha_{\rm aff}\Delta x^{\rm aff})^T(z+\alpha_{\rm aff}\Delta z^{\rm aff})/n\), and choose \(\sigma=(\mu_{\rm aff}/\mu)^3\). Resolve the Newton system with complementarity equation \[Z\Delta x+X\Delta z=\sigma\mu e-XZe-\Delta X^{\rm aff}\Delta z^{\rm aff}.\] Take fraction-to-boundary primal and dual steps, update the iterate, and stop when feasibility and complementarity tolerances hold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Predictor-corrector algorithm for convex quadratic programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full iteration using an affine predictor, cubic adaptive centering, the corrected direction, and a common fraction-to-the-boundary step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \((x_0,y_0,\lambda_0)\) with \((y_0,\lambda_0)>0\). At iteration \(k\), solve the primal-dual Newton system with \(\sigma=0\) for \((\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}},\Delta y^{\mathrm{aff}},\Delta\lambda^{\mathrm{aff}})\); set \(\mu=y^T\lambda/m\) and \[\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{aff}}=\max\{\alpha\in(0,1]:(y,\lambda)+\alpha(\Delta y^{\mathrm{aff}},\Delta\lambda^{\mathrm{aff}})\ge0\},\] \[\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}=\frac{(y+\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta y^{\mathrm{aff}})^T(\lambda+\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta\lambda^{\mathrm{aff}})}{m},\qquad \sigma=\left(\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}}{\mu}\right)^3.\] Solve the corrected predictor-corrector system for \((\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta\lambda)\). Choose \(\tau_k\in(0,1)\), set \(\widehat\alpha=\min\{\alpha_{\tau_k}^{\mathrm{pri}},\alpha_{\tau_k}^{\mathrm{dual}}\}\), and update \[(x_{k+1},y_{k+1},\lambda_{k+1})=(x_k,y_k,\lambda_k)+\widehat\alpha(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta\lambda).\]

assumptions_latex: \alpha_{\tau_k}^{\mathrm{pri}},\alpha_{\tau_k}^{\mathrm{dual}}\ \text{are the fraction-to-the-boundary limits defined for the primal and dual variables}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The iteration generates adaptively centered predictor-corrector QP steps while retaining strict positivity of the slack and multiplier iterates.}

knowledge_statements.title: Augmented KKT Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric indefinite reduction of the primal-dual Newton equations for standard-form convex QPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the Newton equations be \(Q\Delta x-A^T\Delta y-\Delta z=-r_d\), \(A\Delta x=-r_p\), and \(Z\Delta x+X\Delta z=-r_c\), where \(x,z\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\). Eliminating \(\Delta z\) and negating the equality row gives the symmetric augmented KKT system \[\begin{pmatrix}Q+X^{-1}Z&-A^T\\-A&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta x\\\Delta y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-r_d-X^{-1}r_c\\r_p\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Delta z=-X^{-1}(r_c+Z\Delta x).\] Thus the three-block Newton equations and the displayed two-block system are algebraically equivalent whenever \(X\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating the bound-multiplier direction and negating the equality row converts the three-block primal-dual Newton equations into a symmetric-indefinite augmented KKT system; the eliminated direction is then recovered by diagonal substitution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The augmented system and the original primal-dual Newton equations are algebraically equivalent.}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the augmented equations are \(H\Delta x-A^T\Delta y=g\) and \(A\Delta x=h\), where \(H=Q+X^{-1}Z\succ0\). Eliminating \(\Delta x=H^{-1}(g+A^T\Delta y)\) yields the normal equations \[(AH^{-1}A^T)\Delta y=h-AH^{-1}g.\] After solving them, recover \(\Delta x\) from the elimination formula and recover \(\Delta z\) from the complementarity equation. If \(A\) has full row rank, then \(AH^{-1}A^T\succ0\), so the normal-equation solution is unique and is equivalent to the augmented-system solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block elimination of local Newton variables into a reduced coupling system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition a Newton system as \[\begin{pmatrix}K_{\ell\ell}&K_{\ell g}\\K_{g\ell}&K_{gg}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta w_\ell\\\Delta w_g\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}r_\ell\\r_g\end{pmatrix},\] where \(K_{\ell\ell}\) is nonsingular and represents variables eliminable independently or locally. Then \(\Delta w_g\) satisfies the condensed system \[(K_{gg}-K_{g\ell}K_{\ell\ell}^{-1}K_{\ell g})\Delta w_g=r_g-K_{g\ell}K_{\ell\ell}^{-1}r_\ell,\] and \(\Delta w_\ell=K_{\ell\ell}^{-1}(r_\ell-K_{\ell g}\Delta w_g)\). The condensed and full systems are equivalent under this nonsingularity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminate locally solvable Newton variables, solve the Schur-complement system in coupling variables, and recover local directions by back-substitution.
assumptions_latex: The displayed block partition conforms to the QP Newton equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condensed solution reconstructs the unique full-system solution whenever the full block system is nonsingular.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of treating a smaller condensed Newton system as automatically cheaper or numerically preferable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Block condensation replaces \(K_{gg}\) by \(S=K_{gg}-K_{g\ell}K_{\ell\ell}^{-1}K_{\ell g}\). Even when the displayed blocks are sparse, the update can be dense because \(K_{\ell\ell}^{-1}\) need not preserve sparsity. Errors in local solves can also be amplified by ill-conditioning and strong coupling. Therefore reduced dimension alone implies neither lower arithmetic cost nor greater numerical stability; those conclusions require favorable local solves, sparsity, and conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A condensed system can be smaller yet denser or less stable. Its benefit depends on cheap accurate local solves and a favorable Schur complement.
assumptions_latex: Condensation is implemented through solves with K_{\ell\ell}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim(S)<\dim(K)\ \text{does not by itself imply a cheaper or more stable solve}.
knowledge_statements.title: Condensation Sparsity and Stability Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural and spectral accounting for symmetric block condensation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\begin{pmatrix}K_{\ell\ell}&K_{\ell g}\\K_{\ell g}^{\mathsf T}&K_{gg}\end{pmatrix}\) be symmetric with nonsingular symmetric \(K_{\ell\ell}\), and let \(S=K_{gg}-K_{\ell g}^{\mathsf T}K_{\ell\ell}^{-1}K_{\ell g}\). Then \(\det K=\det(K_{\ell\ell})\det S\) and \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(K_{\ell\ell})+\operatorname{inertia}(S)\). Consequently, \(K\) is nonsingular exactly when \(S\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For symmetric condensation, determinants factor and inertias add across the eliminated block and Schur complement, so singularity and spectral signs are preserved exactly.

notation.meaning: Positive, negative, and zero eigenvalue counts of a symmetric matrix.

children.title: Temporally Structured QP Systems
children.top_down_role: Newton systems with stagewise, horizon-based, or dynamic coupling.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic and retained-factor storage for dense-front block-tridiagonal elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the dense elimination front at stage \(t\) has dimension \(d_t\), sequential temporal elimination uses \[O\!\left(\sum_{t=0}^{T}d_t^3\right)\] arithmetic and \[O\!\left(\sum_{t=0}^{T}d_t^2\right)\] retained-factor storage. If \(d_t\le d\), these bounds become \(O(Td^3)\) work and \(O(Td^2)\) storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For bounded stage dimensions, block-tridiagonal temporal elimination has work and retained-factor storage linear in the horizon.
assumptions_latex: The reduced Newton matrix is block tridiagonal.
\(d_t\) is the dense frontal dimension at stage \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_t\le d\Rightarrow O(Td^3)\text{ work and }O(Td^2)\text{ retained-factor storage}.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizon Complexity of Temporal Elimination

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural and pivot limits of the nearest-neighbor unregularized recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A coupling block between stages \(i\) and \(j\) with \(|i-j|>1\) widens the temporal elimination front and can create fill across intervening stages, so the block-tridiagonal recursion and its stated fixed-stage bound no longer apply. Separately, a singular required pivot makes the unregularized recursion undefined, although pivoting, regularization, or a rank-revealing full-space solve may still succeed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Long-range coupling invalidates the nearest-neighbor recursion, while a singular stage pivot stops its unregularized form.
assumptions_latex: Variables are eliminated in temporal order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Long-range coupling widens the front; a singular required pivot stops the unregularized recursion.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Temporal condensation of stage-separable primal-dual Newton equations with nearest-neighbor dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a horizon QP whose objective and barrier blocks are stage separable and whose only interstage constraints link stages \(t\) and \(t+1\), stage ordering makes the augmented Newton matrix block banded. Eliminating nonsingular stage-local primal and inequality blocks produces a block-tridiagonal system in dynamics multipliers. Block \(LDL^T\) elimination, equivalently a Riccati recursion, followed by backward substitution returns the same Newton direction as the unreduced system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearest-neighbor stage coupling yields a block-tridiagonal condensed system whose block elimination is a Riccati-style forward-backward solve.

Interstage constraints couple only consecutive stages.
Every local block required by the unpivoted recursion is nonsingular.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-tridiagonal Newton systems arising from stagewise dynamics coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a horizon-indexed QP whose objective and barrier terms are stage separable and whose only interstage constraints are linear dynamics linking stages \(t\) and \(t+1\), order the Newton variables by stage. The resulting augmented KKT matrix is block banded; eliminating stage-local primal and inequality variables yields a block-tridiagonal system in the dynamics multipliers. Block Gaussian elimination, equivalently a Riccati recursion, computes its solution by a forward factorization and backward substitution. If every required pivot block is nonsingular, this recursion produces exactly the Newton direction of the unreduced KKT system while storing only adjacent-stage coupling blocks.

children.title: Network-Structured QP Systems
children.top_down_role: Newton systems organized around graph incidence or flow structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact consistency and uniqueness conditions for the incidence Schur system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) are the graph's connected components, then \[\ker L=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1_{C_1},\ldots,\mathbf1_{C_k}\},\qquad \operatorname{range}L=\{r:\mathbf1_{C_j}^Tr=0\ \forall j\}.\] Hence \(L\Delta y=r\) is solvable exactly when the residual sums to zero on every component. One independent gauge per component gives a unique representative; a single global gauge is insufficient when \(k>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted-Laplacian equation is consistent exactly when its right-hand side sums to zero on every connected component, and uniqueness requires one gauge per component.
knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Compatibility and Gauges

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-based condensation of separable arc blocks in a primal-dual Newton system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a Newton block system with an invertible positive-definite arc block \(D\) and node-arc coupling \(B\). Eliminating the arc direction produces \[L\Delta y=r,\qquad L=BD^{-1}B^T=BWB^T,\quad W:=D^{-1}\succ0.\] The eliminated arc direction is recovered by substitution. Thus the node-multiplier Schur complement is a weighted graph Laplacian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating a positive-definite separable arc block produces a weighted graph-Laplacian system in node multipliers, followed by local arc recovery.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is an oriented node-arc incidence matrix.
\(D\) is diagonal and positive definite, with \(W=D^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L=BWB^T\succeq0\text{ is the node-multiplier Schur complement.}

Network-Structured QP Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-based Schur complements for network-coupled interior-point Newton equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be an oriented node-arc incidence matrix and suppose elimination of separable arc variables gives a positive diagonal weight matrix \(W\). The multiplier Schur complement is \(L=BWB^T\), and the reduced Newton equation has the form \[L\Delta y=r.\] The matrix \(L\) is a weighted graph Laplacian: it is positive semidefinite and its nullspace consists of vectors constant on each connected component. For a connected network, fixing one node multiplier or imposing \(e^T\Delta y=0\) makes the reduced system nonsingular; the eliminated arc directions are then recovered locally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating separable arc variables produces a weighted graph-Laplacian system in node multipliers, uniquely solvable after removing the componentwise constant nullspace.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the oriented incidence matrix of the network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(BWB^T\succeq0\), with one constant null vector per connected component.

children.title: Slack-Multiplier Scaling
children.top_down_role: Diagonal scaling families induced by interior complementarity variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning boundary for diagonal slack-multiplier scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,z\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), define \(D=X^{1/2}Z^{-1/2}\). Then \(\kappa_2(D)=\sqrt{\max_i(x_i/z_i)/\min_i(x_i/z_i)}\) and \(\kappa_2(D^{-2})=\max_i(z_i/x_i)/\min_i(z_i/x_i)=\kappa_2(D)^2\). Hence scaling quality is determined by the spread of the component ratios, not by the absolute magnitude of complementarity alone. Proportional decay of all pairs can leave \(D\) well-conditioned, whereas a diverging ratio spread makes it ill-conditioned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slack-multiplier scaling is governed by the spread of slack-to-multiplier ratios. Extreme ratio spreads make both the scaling and its induced augmented diagonal term ill-conditioned.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Ratio Conditioning Boundary
Slack-Multiplier Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal scalings induced by positive complementary primal and dual variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For componentwise positive complementary variables \(x,z\in\mathbb R^n_{++}\), define \(D=X^{1/2}Z^{-1/2}\) and \(W=D^2=XZ^{-1}\). Then \(X^{-1}Z=D^{-2}\), and the complementarity linearization \(Z\Delta x+X\Delta z=r_c\) is equivalent to \[D^{-1}\Delta x+D\Delta z=(XZ)^{-1/2}r_c.\] Hence slack-multiplier scaling converts unequal diagonal coefficients into a symmetrically scaled equation and exposes the positive diagonal term \(D^{-2}\) appearing in augmented QP Newton systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive slack and multiplier values define a diagonal scaling that balances the complementarity equation and identifies the diagonal regularization in the augmented Newton matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled and unscaled complementarity equations are equivalent, and \(D^{-2}=X^{-1}Z\succ0\).

children.title: Short-Step Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Tightly centered path-following regimes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-equivalence relations between Euclidean and componentwise complementarity neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=XZe-\mu e\), where \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}z/n\), and define \(\mathcal N_\infty(\gamma)=\{(x,z)>0:\|r\|_\infty\le\gamma\mu\}\). For every \(\theta\ge0\), \[\mathcal N_2(\theta)\subseteq\mathcal N_\infty(\theta),\qquad \mathcal N_\infty(\theta/\sqrt n)\subseteq\mathcal N_2(\theta).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean neighborhood implies the same-radius componentwise neighborhood, while a componentwise radius smaller by the square root of the dimension implies the Euclidean neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean and Componentwise Neighborhood Nesting

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonic dependence of the Euclidean complementarity neighborhood on its radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal N_2(\theta)=\{(x,z)>0:\|XZe-\mu e\|_2\le\theta\mu\}\), parameters \(0\le\theta_1\le\theta_2\) satisfy \[\mathcal N_2(\theta_1)\subseteq\mathcal N_2(\theta_2).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smaller Euclidean radius defines a smaller, more tightly centered short-step neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Nesting of Euclidean Short-Step Neighborhoods

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diagonal Rescaling Invariance of Euclidean Short-Step Membership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of complementarity-residual centrality under reciprocal component scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,z\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), let \(R\succ0\) be diagonal, and set \(\widehat x=Rx\), \(\widehat z=R^{-1}z\). Then \(\widehat X\widehat Ze=XZe\) and \(\widehat\mu=\mu\). Hence, for every \(\theta\ge0\), \[(x,z)\in\mathcal N_2(\theta)\iff(\widehat x,\widehat z)\in\mathcal N_2(\theta).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reciprocal diagonal scaling preserves the complementarity residual and Euclidean short-step membership.
knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal Rescaling Invariance of Euclidean Short-Step Membership

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical fixed-convention definition and componentwise consequence of the Euclidean complementarity neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,z\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), let \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}z/n\), \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), and \(Z=\operatorname{Diag}(z)\). For \(0\le\theta<1\), define \[\mathcal N_2(\theta)=\{(x,z):\|XZe-\mu e\|_2\le\theta\mu\}.\] Membership implies \(|x_i z_i-\mu|\le\theta\mu\) and hence \((1-\theta)\mu\le x_i z_i\le(1+\theta)\mu\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean short-step neighborhood keeps the full complementarity-product vector close to its average and therefore bounds every product on both sides.

notation.meaning: Euclidean short-step neighborhood under the stated convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Short-Step Complementarity Neighborhood
Short-Step Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean central-path neighborhood imposing tight componentwise aggregate centering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,z\in\mathbb R^n_{++}\), let \(\mu=x^Tz/n\). Given \(\theta\in(0,1)\), the short-step neighborhood is \[\mathcal N_2(\theta)=\{(x,z):\|XZe-\mu e\|_2\le\theta\mu\}.\] Membership requires every complementarity product to remain close, in aggregate Euclidean norm, to their average. In particular, \(|x_iz_i-\mu|\le\theta\mu\) for every \(i\), so \((1-\theta)\mu\le x_iz_i\le(1+\theta)\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A short-step iterate is strictly positive and keeps the vector of complementarity products within a small Euclidean distance of its average value.

children.title: Long-Step Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Broader path neighborhoods permitting more aggressive progress.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact componentwise upper and lower consequences of the one-sided long-step condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_i=s_iz_i>0\), \(\mu=n^{-1}\sum_i p_i\), and suppose \(p_i\ge\gamma\mu\) for every \(i\), where \(0<\gamma<1\). Then \(\gamma\mu\le p_i\le[n-(n-1)\gamma]\mu\). Both bounds are sharp: one product may equal \([n-(n-1)\gamma]\mu\) while all remaining products equal \(\gamma\mu\). Consequently no upper bound \(p_i\le C\mu\) with \(C\) independent of dimension follows from one-sided membership alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A long-step neighborhood gives a sharp dimension-dependent upper bound on each complementarity product but no dimension-independent two-sided centrality bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Product Range in a Long-Step Neighborhood
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Product Range in a Long-Step Neighborhood

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonic dependence of the one-sided complementarity neighborhood on its lower-product parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{(s,z)>0:s_iz_i\ge\gamma\mu\ \forall i\}\), where \(\mu=s^{\mathsf T}z/n\), parameters \(0<\gamma_1\le\gamma_2<1\) satisfy \[\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma_2)\subseteq\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma_1).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A larger lower-product parameter defines a smaller, more central long-step neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Nesting of One-Sided Long-Step Neighborhoods

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diagonal Rescaling Invariance of Long-Step Membership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of one-sided complementarity centrality under reciprocal component scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s,z\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), let \(R\succ0\) be diagonal, and define \(\widehat s=Rs\), \(\widehat z=R^{-1}z\). Then \(\widehat s_i\widehat z_i=s_iz_i\) for every \(i\) and \(\widehat\mu=\mu\). Consequently, for every \(0<\gamma<1\), \[(s,z)\in\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\iff(\widehat s,\widehat z)\in\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reciprocal diagonal rescaling of slack and multiplier coordinates preserves all complementarity products and long-step membership.
knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal Rescaling Invariance of Long-Step Membership

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical fixed-convention definition and membership test for a broad one-sided complementarity neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(s,z\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), set \(\mu=s^{\mathsf T}z/n\). For \(0<\gamma<1\), define \[\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{(s,z):s_i z_i\ge\gamma\mu\ \text{for every }i\}.\] Equivalently, \((s,z)\in\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\) if and only if \(\min_i(s_i z_i/\mu)\ge\gamma\). The definition imposes no independent upper-product constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-sided long-step neighborhood keeps every complementarity product above a fixed fraction of average complementarity, without separately imposing an upper bound.

notation.meaning: One-sided long-step neighborhood under the stated convention.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Long-Step Complementarity Neighborhood
Long-Step Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided complementarity neighborhood permitting widely unequal products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,z\in\mathbb R^n_{++}\), let \(\mu=x^Tz/n\). Given \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), define the long-step neighborhood \[\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{(x,z):x_iz_i\ge\gamma\mu\ \text{for all }i=1,\ldots,n\}.\] Unlike a two-sided short-step neighborhood, this condition supplies only a lower bound on each complementary product. Consequently, individual products may exceed \(\mu\) substantially while no component is allowed to approach zero faster than the average complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A long-step iterate remains positive and bounds every complementarity product below by a fixed fraction of the average, without imposing a comparable upper bound.

children.title: Fraction-to-the-Boundary Safeguards
children.top_down_role: Positivity-preserving step-control families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between the first boundary-hitting step and a strict fraction of it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v>0\) and direction \(d\), set \[\alpha_{\max}=\min\left\{1,\min_{d_i<0}\frac{-v_i}{d_i}\right\}.\] Then \(v+\alpha d>0\) for \(0\le\alpha<\alpha_{\max}\). If \(\alpha_{\max}<1\), at least one component of \(v+\alpha_{\max}d\) is zero. Hence a factor \(\tau<1\) preserves strict positivity, whereas \(\tau=1\) may preserve only nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The first boundary-hitting step can make a component zero; a strict fraction preserves interiority.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0<\tau<1\implies v+\tau\alpha_{\max}d>0;\quad \tau=1\text{ may yield a zero component}.

notation.meaning: first boundary-hitting step capped at one

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Positivity Boundary at Unit Fraction
Fraction-to-the-Boundary Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise step truncation preserving strict positivity of interior variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x,z>0\), a direction \((\Delta x,\Delta z)\), and \(\tau\in(0,1)\), define \[\alpha_x=\min\left\{1,\tau\min_{\Delta x_i<0}\frac{-x_i}{\Delta x_i}\right\},\qquad \alpha_z=\min\left\{1,\tau\min_{\Delta z_i<0}\frac{-z_i}{\Delta z_i}\right\},\] with the minimum over an empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). Update \(x^+=x+\alpha_x\Delta x\) and \(z^+=z+\alpha_z\Delta z\), or use the common step \(\alpha=\min\{\alpha_x,\alpha_z\}\). Stop-step computation returns these values before the iterate update. Because \(\tau<1\), every updated component remains strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limit each primal and dual step to a fixed fraction of the first boundary-hitting step, thereby retaining strict positivity after the update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^+>0\) and \(z^+>0\); the same holds under the common step \(\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Primal and dual safeguarded step lengths.

knowledge_statements.title: Centering Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual centering parameter selection for a convex QP Newton step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the convex QP with complementarity variables \(x,z>0\), let \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}z/n\), choose \(\sigma\in[0,1]\), and compute a primal-dual Newton direction whose complementarity equation is \[Z\Delta x+X\Delta z=\sigma\mu e-XZe.\] Choose \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) so that \(x+\alpha\Delta x>0\), \(z+\alpha\Delta z>0\), and the prescribed central neighborhood is retained. Set \((x^+,z^+)=(x,z)+\alpha(\Delta x,\Delta z)\). Larger \(\sigma\) emphasizes recentering; stopping occurs when the chosen primal, dual, and complementarity tolerances hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a centering target, solve the corresponding complementarity Newton equation, and take a positivity-preserving step that remains in the selected central neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\succeq0\) and the primal-dual Newton system is solvable.

children.title: Residual-Reduction Control

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Affine Residual Scaling Along a Newton Step

children.title: Central-Neighborhood Invariance
children.top_down_role: Path-neighborhood structure used to organize iteration analysis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric and one-sided componentwise neighborhoods used in primal-dual path-following analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For positive slack and multiplier vectors \(x,z\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) and \(\mu=x^Tz/n\), define \[\mathcal N_\infty(\theta)=\{(x,z):\|XZe-\mu e\|_\infty\leq\theta\mu\},\quad 0\leq\theta<1,\] and \[\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)=\{(x,z):x_i z_i\geq\gamma\mu\ \text{for every }i\},\quad 0<\gamma<1.\] Membership in \(\mathcal N_\infty(\theta)\) is equivalent to \((1-\theta)\mu\leq x_i z_i\leq(1+\theta)\mu\) for every \(i\), whereas \(\mathcal N_{-\infty}(\gamma)\) imposes only the lower componentwise bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric neighborhoods bound every complementarity product above and below its mean, while wide one-sided neighborhoods impose only a uniform lower fraction of the mean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed norm and componentwise inequalities define the symmetric and one-sided central-neighborhood variants.
knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Central-Neighborhood Variants

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete loss of a symmetric componentwise neighborhood under an unrestricted positive update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start at \(x=z=(1,1)\), which belongs to \(\mathcal N_\infty(\theta)\) for every \(\theta\ge0\). For \(0<\epsilon<1\), set \(x^+=(\epsilon,1)\) and \(z^+=(1,1)\). Then \(x^+,z^+>0\), but \(\mu^+=(1+\epsilon)/2\) and \[\frac{\|X^+Z^+e-\mu^+e\|_\infty}{\mu^+}=\frac{1-\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}.\] Hence the positive update leaves \(\mathcal N_\infty(\theta)\) whenever \(\epsilon<(1-\theta)/(1+\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An update can preserve positivity while making complementarity products too imbalanced for the central neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Positivity Does Not Preserve Centrality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration consequence of an assumed neighborhood-specific contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(w^0\in\mathcal N(\theta)\), every update maps \(\mathcal N(\theta)\) into itself, and \(\mu_{k+1}\le(1-\eta)\mu_k\) for fixed \(\eta\in(0,1)\), then \(\mu_k\le(1-\eta)^k\mu_0\). Thus \(k\ge\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)/[-\log(1-\eta)]\) suffices for \(\mu_k\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Neighborhood invariance plus uniform contraction gives geometric complementarity convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Invariant Contraction Consequence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceptance test for the complementarity component of a proposed update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s^+,z^+>0\) and \(\mu^+=(s^+)^{\mathsf T}z^+/m\). The complementarity condition of \(\mathcal N_\infty(\theta)\) holds exactly when \((1-\theta)\mu^+\le s_i^+z_i^+\le(1+\theta)\mu^+\) for every \(i\). For a Euclidean neighborhood it holds exactly when \(\|S^+z^+-\mu^+e\|_2\le\theta\mu^+\). Full neighborhood membership additionally requires every affine-feasibility condition in that neighborhood's definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Centrality can be checked after an update, but this test alone neither verifies omitted affine equations nor guarantees a step bounded away from zero.
knowledge_statements.title: A Posteriori Complementarity-Neighborhood Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic identity underlying one-step invariance tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(s^+=s+\alpha\Delta s\) and \(z^+=z+\alpha\Delta z\), \[S^+z^+=Sz+\alpha(Z\Delta s+S\Delta z)+\alpha^2(\Delta s\circ\Delta z).\] If \(Z\Delta s+S\Delta z=\sigma\mu e-Sz\), then \[S^+z^+=(1-\alpha)Sz+\alpha\sigma\mu e+\alpha^2(\Delta s\circ\Delta z).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The updated complementarity vector is its linear centered target plus an explicit quadratic direction product.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s,z\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\), \(\mu=s^{\mathsf T}z/m\), and suppose \(\|SZe-\mu e\|_p<\theta\mu\) for \(p\in\{2,\infty\}\) and \(0<\theta<1\). For finite directions \(\Delta s,\Delta z\), define \(s(\alpha)=s+\alpha\Delta s\), \(z(\alpha)=z+\alpha\Delta z\), and \(\mu(\alpha)=s(\alpha)^{\mathsf T}z(\alpha)/m\). Then some \(\bar\alpha>0\) satisfies, for every \(\alpha\in[0,\bar\alpha]\), \(s(\alpha),z(\alpha)>0\) and \(\|S(\alpha)Z(\alpha)e-\mu(\alpha)e\|_p\leq\theta\mu(\alpha)\).

Initialization Regimes for Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three starting-point models used in polynomial interior-point analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Complexity analyses distinguish three initialization regimes. In the feasible-start regime, the input includes \((x^0,y^0,z^0)\) satisfying \(Ax^0=b\), \(Qx^0+c-A^{\mathsf T}y^0-z^0=0\), and \(x^0,z^0>0\). In the infeasible-start regime, only \(x^0,z^0>0\) is required and primal-dual residuals are driven to zero together with complementarity. In an embedded regime, the QP is enlarged by homogeneous or artificial variables so that an explicit strictly interior initial point exists; the embedding’s terminal solution yields an optimal solution or an infeasibility certificate for the original QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complexity may assume a strictly feasible start, reduce feasibility residuals from an interior start, or use an embedding with an explicit interior start.

The selected embedding, when used, preserves the original solution or certificate interpretation.

children.title: Input Encoding Size
children.top_down_role: Bit-length and data-representation regimes used to measure problem size.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of finite binary input-size analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Turing input-size parameter \(L\) is defined only for data having a finite effective encoding. Arbitrary exact real coefficients supplied without rational, algebraic, oracle, or approximation encodings have no finite binary length, so a runtime claimed polynomial in \(L\) is undefined for that input model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact arbitrary real coefficients have no Turing input size unless an effective finite or oracle representation is specified.
assumptions_latex: Complexity is asserted in the Turing bit model
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite encoding model for every coefficient is necessary before polynomial bit complexity can be stated.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense and Sparse QP Encoding Sizes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural contributions of dense-array and sparse coordinate or compressed representations to rational-QP input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) and \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), a dense representation has \(\Theta(n^2+mn+m+n)\) scalar slots before coefficient bit lengths are summed. A conventional sparse representation stores \(\operatorname{nnz}(Q)+\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n\) scalar values together with indices or pointer arrays whose bit length is polynomial in \(m,n\), and the number of stored entries. Thus the structural contribution to \(L\) depends on whether zero entries are explicit and on the declared sparse format; symmetry storage changes only representation-dependent factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense length counts matrix slots, whereas sparse length counts stored values plus indices and pointers; the representation determining input length must be declared.
assumptions_latex: QP coefficients have finite binary encodings
A fixed dense-array or sparse binary representation is used
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dense and sparse encodings may assign different structural input lengths to the same mathematical QP.

Input Encoding Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary length of rational convex-QP data in the Turing model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational data \(Q,A,b,c\), write every scalar in lowest terms as \(p/q\), with \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(q\in\mathbb N\), and define \(\ell(p/q)=1+\lceil\log_2(1+|p|)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(1+q)\rceil\). The input encoding size is \[L=\sum_{u\in(Q,A,b,c)}\ell(u)+L_{\mathrm{dim}},\] where \(L_{\mathrm{dim}}\) records the dimensions and array delimiters under a fixed binary encoding. An algorithm is polynomial in input size only when its bit-operation count and intermediate operand lengths are polynomially bounded in \(L\) and the requested output precision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The input size is the total binary length of all reduced rational coefficients, dimensions, and structural delimiters under a fixed encoding.
assumptions_latex: All QP coefficients are rational and represented in binary.
A fixed unambiguous array encoding is used.

children.title: Precision-Complexity Interface
children.top_down_role: Dependence of complexity claims on numerical precision and accuracy conventions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of polynomial precision complexity on the representation of a binary accuracy request.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\), \(p\geq0\). Under the ordinary rational encoding of \(\varepsilon\), the denominator \(2^p\) has \(\Theta(p)\) binary digits, so a runtime polynomial in \(p=\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\) is polynomial in the encoded tolerance length, whereas a runtime polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon=2^p\) is exponential in that length. If instead the tolerance is supplied succinctly by storing only the exponent \(p\) in binary, its literal encoding has \(\Theta(\log(1+p))\) bits, and polynomial dependence on \(p\) is not polynomial in that succinct encoding length unless the complexity convention explicitly treats \(p\) as the precision parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Logarithmic dependence on inverse tolerance is polynomial for an ordinary binary rational tolerance, while succinct exponent encodings require separate accounting.
assumptions_latex: The representation of the requested tolerance is declared
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The distinction between \(\operatorname{poly}(\log(1/\varepsilon))\) and \(\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon)\) establishes precision polynomiality only relative to the stated accuracy encoding.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Long-Step Neighborhood Allows Large Component Imbalance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Family-specific geometric boundary of the broad one-sided neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_i=x_i z_i>0\), \(\mu=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\), and suppose \(p_i\ge\beta\mu\) for every \(i\), where \(0<\beta<1\). Then \(p_i\le[n-(n-1)\beta]\mu\) for every \(i\), and equality is possible by taking the other \(n-1\) products equal to \(\beta\mu\). Thus this neighborhood permits a componentwise product of order \(n\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-sided long-step neighborhood prevents very small complementarity products but may allow one product to be order n times the average.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i p_i/\mu\le n-(n-1)\beta\), and equality is attainable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positivity Gives No Global Potential Lower Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling boundary for the logarithmic primal-dual potential with parameter \(\rho>m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Phi_\rho(s,z)=\rho\log(s^{\mathsf T}z)-\sum_{i=1}^m\log(s_i z_i)\) and any \(\tau>0\), \[\Phi_\rho(\tau s,z)=\Phi_\rho(s,z)+(\rho-m)\log\tau.\] Thus, when \(\rho>m\), letting \(\tau\downarrow0\) makes \(\Phi_\rho(\tau s,z)\to-\infty\) despite \(\tau s,z>0\). Positivity alone therefore cannot supply the finite nonterminal lower bound needed to telescope a uniform potential decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithmic potential is unbounded below over the positive orthant, so a complexity proof needs a termination-dependent or invariant-set lower bound.

notation.meaning: Positive scaling of one complementarity vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Positivity Gives No Global Potential Lower Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite lower bound before a complementarity target is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\rho>m\), \(s,z>0\), and \(\mu=(s^{\mathsf T}z)/m>\varepsilon>0\), \[\Phi_\rho(s,z)\ge(\rho-m)\log(m\varepsilon)+m\log m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive complementarity stopping threshold supplies a finite nonterminal lower bound, although positivity alone does not.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Nonterminal Potential Lower Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential Imbalance Controls the Smallest Complementarity Product
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Centrality consequence of bounding the shape component of the potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_i=s_i z_i>0\), \(q_i=mp_i/\sum_jp_j\), and \(D=-\sum_i\log q_i\). Since \(q_i\le m\), \[D\le B\Rightarrow s_i z_i\ge e^{-B}m^{-(m-1)}\mu\quad\text{for every }i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded imbalance term prevents any complementarity product from vanishing relative to the mean.
knowledge_statements.title: Potential Imbalance Controls the Smallest Complementarity Product

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scale-Imbalance Decomposition of the Logarithmic Potential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact decomposition separating complementarity scale from imbalance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_i=s_i z_i>0\), \(t=\sum_i p_i=m\mu\), and \(q_i=mp_i/t\). Then \[\Phi_\rho(s,z)=(\rho-m)\log t+m\log m-\sum_{i=1}^m\log q_i.\] The last term is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when every \(p_i=\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The potential separates into a complementarity-scale term and a nonnegative imbalance term vanishing on the central path.

notation.meaning: Complementarity product normalized to mean one.

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Imbalance Decomposition of the Logarithmic Potential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a logarithmic-potential bound into an average-complementarity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\rho>m\), \(s,z\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\), and \(\mu=s^{\mathsf T}z/m\), \[\Phi_\rho(s,z)\le B\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mu\le \frac1m\exp\!\left(\frac{B-m\log m}{\rho-m}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper bound on the logarithmic potential supplies an explicit upper bound on average complementarity.

notation.meaning: Certified upper bound on the potential.

knowledge_statements.title: Potential Upper Bound Certifies Complementarity
Potential-Reduction Complexity Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional feasible-start potential-reduction iteration bound for a convex QP with inequality slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For complementarity pairs \(s^k,z^k\in\mathbb R_{++}^{m}\), let \(\mu_k=(s^k)^{\mathsf T}z^k/m\) and \[\Phi_\rho(s,z)=\rho\log(s^{\mathsf T}z)-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log(s_i z_i),\qquad \rho>m.\] Suppose each nonterminal iteration satisfies \(\Phi_\rho(s^{k+1},z^{k+1})\le \Phi_\rho(s^k,z^k)-\delta\) for some \(\delta>0\), and suppose a finite constant \(L_\varepsilon\) satisfies \(\Phi_\rho(s^k,z^k)\ge L_\varepsilon\) whenever \(\mu_k>\varepsilon\). Then the first index \(N\) for which \(\mu_N\le\varepsilon\) satisfies \[N\le \left\lceil\frac{\Phi_\rho(s^0,z^0)-L_\varepsilon}{\delta}\right\rceil.\] In particular, if \(\Phi_\rho(s^0,z^0)-L_\varepsilon=O\!\left(\delta\sqrt m\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right)\), then \(N=O\!\left(\sqrt m\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform potential decrease gives an iteration bound only when the potential has a finite lower bound along all nonterminal iterates. A square-root logarithmic rate additionally requires the corresponding bound on the initial potential gap.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\succeq0\) and a strictly feasible primal-dual starting point exists.
The potential decreases by at least \(\delta>0\), and \(L_\varepsilon\) is a finite lower bound on the nonterminal potentials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\le\left\lceil(\Phi_\rho(s^0,z^0)-L_\varepsilon)/\delta\right\rceil\), with the stated conditional polynomial specialization.

notation.meaning: Finite lower bound for the potential over nonterminal iterates.

children.title: Optimality-Certificate Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Optimality-Certificate Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration and sparse-arithmetic verification costs for an approximate KKT certificate of a convex QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^p\), \(G\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(h\in\mathbb R^m\). Consider \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\ \tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\quad Gx+s=h,\quad s\ge0.\] An absolute \(\varepsilon\)-KKT certificate is a tuple \((x,y,s,z)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m\) with \(s,z\ge0\) satisfying \[\max\!\left\{\|Ax-b\|,\|Gx+s-h\|,\|Qx+c+A^{\mathsf T}y+G^{\mathsf T}z\|,s^{\mathsf T}z\right\}\le\varepsilon.\] A short-step primal-dual path-following method initialized in its prescribed neighborhood and having the standard contraction bound produces such a certificate after \[O\!\left(\sqrt m\log\frac{m\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\right)\] iterations, because the gap condition requires average complementarity at most \(\varepsilon/m\). Given the tuple, verification costs \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(Q)+\operatorname{nnz}(A)+\operatorname{nnz}(G)+n+p+m)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A short-step method reaches an absolute KKT-gap tolerance after a square-root logarithmic number of iterations, with the logarithm adjusted because the total gap equals m times average complementarity. The supplied certificate is checked using sparse matrix-vector products and vector operations.
assumptions_latex: A strictly feasible primal-dual point in the short-step neighborhood is available.
The method satisfies its stated short-step complementarity contraction, and the residual norm is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N=O\!\left(\sqrt m\log(m\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right)\), and certificate verification is linear in the stored matrix nonzeros up to vector operations.

notation.meaning: Primal variables, equality multipliers, slacks, and inequality multipliers.
Absolute residual and total complementarity tolerance.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: total complementarity equals m times average complementarity

children.title: Infeasibility-Certificate Complexity
children.top_down_role: Iteration regimes for producing approximate evidence of primal or dual infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes a validated infeasibility certificate from a merely small numerical Farkas residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\) and \(Gx\le h\), vectors \((y,z)\) with \(z\ge0\), \(b^{\mathsf T}y+h^{\mathsf T}z=-1\), and \(A^{\mathsf T}y+G^{\mathsf T}z=0\) certify infeasibility. If only \(\|A^{\mathsf T}y+G^{\mathsf T}z\|\le\varepsilon\) is known, the uncancelled term \(x^{\mathsf T}(A^{\mathsf T}y+G^{\mathsf T}z)\) need not be controlled when no bound on a putative feasible \(x\) is available. Thus a small cancellation residual alone is not an exact infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized multiplier with a small but nonzero cancellation residual is not automatically an exact infeasibility certificate; rigorous validation or an applicable error bound is required.
assumptions_latex: No a priori bound controls the residual inner product with a putative feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|A^{\mathsf T}y+G^{\mathsf T}z\|\le\varepsilon\ \text{alone does not certify exact infeasibility.}
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Farkas Residual Boundary
Infeasibility-Certificate Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generation and direct verification boundary for a Farkas certificate of primal infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the constraint system \(Ax=b\), \(Gx\le h\), an exact primal-infeasibility certificate is a pair \((y,z)\) satisfying \[A^{\mathsf T}y+G^{\mathsf T}z=0,\qquad z\ge0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y+h^{\mathsf T}z<0.\] After normalization \(b^{\mathsf T}y+h^{\mathsf T}z=-1\), verification costs \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+\operatorname{nnz}(G)+m+n)\) arithmetic operations. If an embedding-based interior-point method has iteration bound \(T(\varepsilon)\) for reaching a normalized certificate residual at most \(\varepsilon\), certificate generation requires at most \(T(\varepsilon)\) iterations; this complexity is not implied by an optimality-only path-following bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized Farkas vector is cheaply verifiable, but polynomial-time generation requires an infeasibility-aware embedding or phase method rather than an optimality-only path follower.
assumptions_latex: The constraint data are finite-dimensional and explicitly represented.
The exact certificate is normalized by \(b^{\mathsf T}y+h^{\mathsf T}z=-1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{verify}}=O(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+\operatorname{nnz}(G)+m+n)\), while generation complexity equals the bound established for the chosen status-detecting method.

notation.meaning: Iteration bound of the selected embedding or phase method.

children.title: Unboundedness-Status Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity considerations for distinguishing unbounded behavior from numerical failure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates verification of a supplied recession ray from algorithmic generation of an unboundedness status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex QP over a nonempty polyhedron, feasible iterates with decreasing objective values, large norms, or failed KKT residuals do not by themselves certify \(\inf f=-\infty\). A rigorous status requires validated recession evidence, such as a feasible base point \(x_0\) and direction \(d\) satisfying \(Ad=0\), \(Gd\le0\), \(Qd=0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\). Therefore an iteration bound proved only for convergence to an optimal primal-dual point gives no unboundedness-detection bound unless the method is separately proved to generate such evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diverging iterates or decreasing objective values are not unboundedness certificates. An optimality-only iteration theorem does not bound production of a validated recession ray.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is a nonempty polyhedron.
No separate status-detection theorem is assumed.

notation.meaning: Feasible base point for the recession ray.

knowledge_statements.title: Unboundedness Detection Boundary
Unboundedness-Status Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse-arithmetic verification complexity for an exact recession certificate of convex-QP unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^p\), \(G\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(h\in\mathbb R^m\). knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Iteration Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Short-step path-following iteration count, distinct from the arithmetic cost of solving Newton systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex QP with \(m\) complementarity pairs, suppose a short-step primal-dual method keeps every iterate in a fixed central-path neighborhood and chooses steps satisfying \[\mu_{k+1}\le\left(1-\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt m}\right)\mu_k\] for a constant \(\gamma\in(0,1)\) independent of the data and \(k\). Then an iterate with \(\mu_k\le\varepsilon\) is obtained after at most \[\left\lceil\frac{\sqrt m}{\gamma}\log\frac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil+1\] iterations. This is an iteration bound only; it does not bound factorization cost, finite-precision bit complexity, or conditioning-dependent work inside an iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform square-root-scaled complementarity contraction yields a logarithmic-accuracy polynomial iteration count but says nothing by itself about linear-system cost.
assumptions_latex: Every iterate remains in the neighborhood for which the contraction estimate holds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation-independent dense cost once a Newton system of fixed order has been assembled.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Once a dense symmetric Newton system of order \(r\) has been assembled, a standard dense direct factorization costs \(O(r^3)\) arithmetic operations and each triangular solution costs \(O(r^2)\). The assembly cost is formulation-dependent and must be accounted for separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense Newton factorization is cubic in the system order, while triangular solves are quadratic; assembly depends on the chosen elimination.
assumptions_latex: A dense unit-cost arithmetic model is used.
A standard dense direct factorization is applicable to the assembled system.

knowledge_statements.title: Generic Dense Direct-Solve Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on sparsity-only operation counts for Newton factorizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sparse symmetric Newton matrix, an elimination ordering generally creates fill. Triangular solution work is proportional to the number of stored factor entries, while factorization work and storage depend on elimination fronts, ordering, and the sparsity graph. Without structural restrictions, the filled factor can be dense, so an order-\(r\) sparse input can still require \(O(r^3)\) factorization work and \(O(r^2)\) storage.

assumptions_latex: A direct symmetric factorization is used.
No graph class or fill guarantee is assumed.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Fill Determines Direct-Solve Cost
Per-Iteration Arithmetic Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense direct-solve cost for one primal-dual Newton iteration after standard block elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a primal-dual QP iteration whose block eliminations produce a dense symmetric Newton system of order \(r=n+p\), where \(n\) is the primal dimension and \(p\) is the number of equality constraints. Forming its coefficient matrix costs at most \(O(n^2m+n m^2)\) arithmetic operations under naive dense multiplication, while a dense symmetric-indefinite factorization and triangular solves cost \(O(r^3)\) and \(O(r^2)\), respectively. Consequently, one iteration has polynomial dense arithmetic cost \[O(n^2m+n m^2+(n+p)^3).\] For sparse implementations, this expression is only an upper bound because actual work depends on ordering and factor fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After eliminating complementarity blocks, a dense Newton step costs cubic work in the reduced system size plus the work required to assemble that system.
assumptions_latex: All matrices are treated as dense and arithmetic operations have unit cost.
The diagonal complementarity blocks are nonsingular because \(s>0\) and \(z>0\).

children.title: Conditioning-Driven Solve Complexity
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic and precision costs arising from difficult Newton-system conditioning.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-accuracy limitation for an inexact Newton-system solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be nonsingular, \(Hd=r\), and \((H+E)\widehat d=r\), with \(\|E\|\le\delta\|H\|\) in a subordinate norm. If \(\kappa(H)\delta<1\), then \(\|\widehat d-d\|/\|d\|\le\kappa(H)\delta/(1-\kappa(H)\delta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditioning amplifies backward error, so a stable solve need not give a uniformly accurate Newton direction when the condition number is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Condition-Number Amplification of Backward Error
Conditioning-Driven Solve Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative solution cost for a symmetric positive-definite reduced Newton system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the reduced Newton equation be \(H_k d=r_k\), where \(H_k\) is symmetric positive definite, and let \(P_k\) be a symmetric positive-definite preconditioner. Preconditioned conjugate gradients returns \(d_j\) satisfying \[\|d_j-d_*\|_{H_k}\le\eta\|d_0-d_*\|_{H_k}\] after \[j=O\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa(P_k^{-1/2}H_kP_k^{-1/2})}\log(1/\eta)\right)\] preconditioned matrix-vector iterations. Thus polynomial outer iteration complexity does not alone imply a uniform arithmetic bound: the inner work also depends on spectral conditioning, preconditioner application cost, and the accuracy \(\eta\) required to preserve the outer neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An iterative Newton solve scales with the square root of the preconditioned condition number and logarithmically with the requested relative accuracy.
assumptions_latex: The stopping criterion is relative error in the \(H_k\)-energy norm.

notation.meaning: Spectral condition number of the preconditioned system.

children.title: Practical Predictor-Corrector Theory Boundary
